lessons.title: Context: The Russian Revolution & Orwell's Purpose
lessons.description: Orwell's political purpose, the Russian Revolution, and why Animal Farm is an allegorical satire.
lessons.content_html:
Why Did Orwell Write Animal Farm?

George Orwell (born Eric Arthur Blair, 1903–1950) was a democratic socialist who believed passionately in equality and freedom. He was not opposed to socialism itself — he was opposed to what happened when revolutionary ideals were hijacked by power-hungry leaders. His experience fighting in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) was the turning point: he witnessed Soviet-backed communists betraying and attacking their own allies, showing him that revolutionary language could be used to disguise totalitarianism.

Key Fact

Orwell wrote Animal Farm in 1943–1944, published in 1945. He subtitled it ‘A Fairy Story’ — an ironic joke, since the novella is a dark political warning about how revolutions can be betrayed by those who seize power.

Orwell struggled to get Animal Farm published because Britain was allied with the Soviet Union during World War II. Several publishers rejected it, fearing it would damage the wartime alliance. This censorship only strengthened Orwell’s belief that uncomfortable truths must be told.

The Russian Revolution: Essential Background

Before 1917, Russia was ruled by Tsar Nicholas II, an autocratic emperor who held absolute power while most of the population lived in desperate poverty. Anger over inequality, food shortages, and Russia’s catastrophic losses in World War I led to two revolutions in 1917. In February, mass protests forced the Tsar to abdicate. In October, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power in a coup. They were inspired by the political philosophy of Karl Marx, who argued that the working class should overthrow the ruling class and share wealth equally.

Lenin led the October Revolution and established the Soviet Union, but he died in 1924 before the new state was fully established. A power struggle followed between Joseph Stalin and Leon Trotsky. Stalin was a cunning political operator who built alliances behind the scenes, while Trotsky was an intellectual and brilliant orator who believed in spreading revolution worldwide. Stalin won, expelled Trotsky from the country in 1929, and eventually had him assassinated in Mexico in 1940. Stalin then ruled the Soviet Union as a dictator through fear, propaganda, purges and a cult of personality.

Stalin’s Soviet Union

Under Stalin, the Soviet Union became a one-party state controlled through terror. The secret police (first the OGPU, then the NKVD) arrested, imprisoned and executed millions. Stalin’s Great Purges of the 1930s targeted anyone suspected of disloyalty — including many of the original Bolsheviks who had fought in the Revolution. Show trials forced victims to confess publicly to fabricated crimes. Meanwhile, state propaganda through the newspaper Pravda (meaning ‘truth’) presented Stalin as a benevolent father figure and rewrote history to erase his rivals, particularly Trotsky. It is this specific pattern — revolution, power struggle, dictatorship, propaganda, purges — that Orwell recreates in Animal Farm.

Allegory, Fable and Satire

Animal Farm works on three literary levels simultaneously. It is a allegory — every character, event and setting maps onto the history of the Russian Revolution and Soviet Union. It is a fable — a simple story with animal characters that conveys a moral message. And it is a satire — using dark humour and irony to attack totalitarianism and expose how power corrupts.

Key Fact

For the Edexcel exam, you need to show understanding of context (AO3). This means connecting events and characters in Animal Farm to the Russian Revolution, Orwell’s political beliefs, and the historical period — not in a separate paragraph, but woven throughout your essay.

A common misconception is that Orwell was attacking communism or socialism. In fact, he described himself as a democratic socialist and wrote in his essay ‘Why I Write’ (1946) that “every line of serious work that I have written since 1936 has been written, directly or indirectly, against totalitarianism and for democratic Socialism.” Animal Farm criticises the betrayal of socialist ideals by authoritarian leaders — it is a warning about how power corrupts, not an argument against equality.

The Publication Controversy

Orwell completed Animal Farm in February 1944, but it took over a year to find a publisher. T.S. Eliot, then a director at Faber & Faber, rejected it on the grounds that it was “not the right point of view from which to criticise the political situation.” Jonathan Cape initially accepted the manuscript but withdrew after a warning from the Ministry of Information. This censorship demonstrated exactly the kind of political suppression Orwell was warning about — even in a democracy, uncomfortable truths about a powerful ally could be silenced. When the book was finally published by Secker & Warburg in August 1945, it became an immediate bestseller and has remained one of the most widely read political texts in the English language.

Why Context Matters for Edexcel

In the Edexcel Component 1 Section B exam, you answer ONE essay question from a choice of two. Each question is preceded by a short quotation from the text as a stimulus. The assessment objectives are AO1 (informed personal response with textual references), AO3 (understanding context) and AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar). There are no AO2 marks for this section, which means you do not need to analyse language techniques in detail — instead, focus on developing a clear argument about characters, themes or events and connecting them to context.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Edexcel Section B is worth 40 marks (AO1 + AO3 + AO4). There is no AO2 in this section, so you do not need to analyse individual words or language techniques. Instead, focus on building a clear argument that references specific moments from the text and connects them to the Russian Revolution and Orwell’s political purpose. Always address the quotation given in the question — it is your starting point, not something to ignore. Use specialist vocabulary like ‘allegory’, ‘totalitarianism’ and ‘propaganda’ to boost your AO4 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Orwell was a democratic socialist who wrote Animal Farm to warn against the corruption of revolutionary ideals under Stalin — not to attack socialism itself.
  • Animal Farm is simultaneously a fable, an allegory of the Russian Revolution, and a satire of totalitarianism.
  • For Edexcel (AO1 + AO3 + AO4), weave contextual knowledge about the Russian Revolution throughout your essay rather than bolting it on as a separate paragraph.

lessons.title: Chapters 1-3: The Rebellion
lessons.description: Old Major's speech, the Seven Commandments, the Battle of the Cowshed and the early hopes of revolution.
lessons.content_html:
Old Major’s Speech: The Spark of Revolution

The novella opens with Old Major, a prize-winning boar, calling the animals together for a secret meeting in the barn. His speech is the catalyst for everything that follows. He tells the animals that “our lives are miserable, laborious, and short” and that Man is the source of all their suffering. His argument is simple and powerful: remove the human oppressor, and the animals will be free and equal.

Key Fact

Old Major represents both Karl Marx (who developed the theory of communism) and Vladimir Lenin (who led the October Revolution). His speech mirrors The Communist Manifesto’s call for workers to overthrow their oppressors. He dies before the revolution happens, just as Marx died before the Russian Revolution.

Old Major teaches the animals the song ‘Beasts of England’, which becomes a revolutionary anthem. The song paints a utopian vision of a future without humans: “rings shall vanish from our noses, and the harness from our back.” This vision of freedom and equality is genuinely moving — Orwell wants the reader to understand why revolution seems so appealing before showing how it can go wrong.

The Rebellion and the Seven Commandments

After Old Major dies, the animals — led by the pigs Napoleon and Snowball — drive Mr Jones from the farm. The speed and ease of the Rebellion mirrors the October Revolution, where the Bolsheviks seized power with relatively little resistance. The animals rename Manor Farm as ‘Animal Farm’ and establish Animalism as their governing philosophy — a direct parallel to Marxism-Leninism.

The pigs condense Old Major’s teachings into the Seven Commandments, painted on the barn wall. These commandments represent the founding principles of the revolution, just as the Soviet constitution promised equality and workers’ rights. The most important is the seventh: “All animals are equal.”

1. Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy. 2. Whatever goes upon four legs, or has wings, is a friend. 3. No animal shall wear clothes. 4. No animal shall sleep in a bed. 5. No animal shall drink alcohol. 6. No animal shall kill any other animal. 7. All animals are equal. These commandments function as both the constitution of Animal Farm and a structural device — Orwell uses their gradual alteration throughout the novella to track the corruption of the revolution.

Early Optimism: The Harvest and the Cowshed

The early chapters of Animal Farm are deliberately hopeful. The animals work harder than they ever did for Jones, but they do so willingly because they believe they are working for themselves. The harvest is “the biggest harvest that the farm had ever seen” — a detail that mirrors the genuine early achievements of Soviet collective farming before Stalin’s disastrous policies took hold.

Key Fact

The Battle of the Cowshed occurs when Jones and neighbouring farmers try to retake the farm. Snowball leads the defence brilliantly, planning military tactics inspired by Julius Caesar. This parallels the Russian Civil War (1918–1921), where Trotsky organised the Red Army to defeat the counter-revolutionary White forces.

Even in these optimistic early chapters, Orwell plants seeds of future corruption. On the very first day after the Rebellion, the cows’ milk mysteriously disappears. The animals later discover that the pigs have been taking the milk and apples for themselves. Squealer justifies this by claiming the pigs need them because they do “brainwork” — and warns that if the pigs fail, “Jones would come back!” This is the first use of propaganda to justify privilege, and it establishes the pattern that will define the rest of the novella: the pigs claim special treatment is for the common good, when it is really for their own benefit.

The Pigs Take Charge

From the very beginning, the pigs position themselves as the natural leaders. They do not do any physical labour during the harvest — instead, they “directed and supervised the others.” The word ‘naturally’ recurs when describing the pigs’ assumption of authority, as though their leadership is inevitable rather than chosen. This mirrors how the Bolshevik intellectuals positioned themselves as the ‘vanguard of the proletariat’ — the educated elite who would lead the revolution on behalf of the workers. Orwell subtly questions this assumption: if the revolution is about equality, why should one group automatically lead? The pigs’ early claim to intellectual superiority is the first crack in Animalism’s promise of equality, and it widens throughout the novella until the hierarchy is as rigid as it was under Jones.

Orwell’s Structural Choices

Orwell structures the opening chapters to create a deliberate arc from hope to warning. The reader shares the animals’ excitement about the Rebellion, making the later betrayal more devastating. The simplicity of the fable form means that every detail carries allegorical weight. The milk and apples are not just food — they represent how revolutionary leaders immediately begin appropriating resources for themselves. For the Edexcel exam, connecting these narrative choices to context will demonstrate the sophisticated understanding that earns higher marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the early chapters, avoid simply retelling the plot. Instead, focus on Orwell’s purpose: why does he make the Rebellion seem so positive? The answer is that he wants the reader to share the animals’ hope so that the subsequent corruption feels more shocking and devastating. This structural choice mirrors how the early Soviet period generated genuine optimism before Stalin’s betrayal. Always connect narrative events to Orwell’s message and the historical context.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Old Major’s speech represents Marx’s and Lenin’s revolutionary ideas; ‘Beasts of England’ is the utopian vision that inspires rebellion.
  • The Seven Commandments are a structural device — their gradual alteration tracks the corruption of the revolution throughout the novella.
  • Even in the hopeful early chapters, the disappearance of the milk and apples foreshadows how the pigs will betray the revolution for personal gain.

lessons.title: Chapters 4-6: Napoleon's Rise
lessons.description: Snowball vs Napoleon, the expulsion of Snowball, Squealer's propaganda and the consolidation of power.
lessons.content_html:
The Power Struggle: Snowball vs Napoleon

After the Rebellion, two pigs emerge as leaders: Snowball and Napoleon. They disagree on virtually everything. Snowball is energetic, eloquent and full of ideas — he organises committees, tries to teach the animals to read, and draws up plans for a windmill that will bring electricity to the farm and reduce the animals’ working hours. Napoleon, by contrast, says little in public debates but works behind the scenes, quietly building his own power base.

Key Fact

Snowball represents Leon Trotsky: an intellectual, a brilliant speaker, and a genuine believer in spreading revolution. Napoleon represents Joseph Stalin: quiet, calculating, and focused on consolidating personal power rather than advancing revolutionary ideals.

The windmill debate is the key conflict. Snowball argues passionately that the windmill will transform the animals’ lives. Napoleon opposes it — not because he has a better plan, but because he cannot allow Snowball to gain popularity. This mirrors the real disagreement between Stalin and Trotsky over industrialisation, but Orwell shows that for Napoleon, the debate is really about power, not policy.

The Expulsion of Snowball

Napoleon’s masterstroke comes at the crucial meeting about the windmill. Just as Snowball is delivering his most persuasive speech, Napoleon gives a “high-pitched whimper” and nine enormous dogs — the puppies he secretly took from their mothers and raised in isolation — burst into the barn and chase Snowball from the farm. This is one of the novella’s most shocking moments. Violence, not argument, decides the power struggle.

The nine dogs represent Stalin’s secret police (the NKVD, later the KGB). Napoleon takes them as puppies and raises them “in a loft” away from the other animals, training them to be loyal only to him. This detail is crucial: Napoleon plans his violent seizure of power long before the windmill debate. The dogs enforce Napoleon’s will through fear, just as Stalin used the secret police to silence, imprison and execute opponents. After Snowball’s expulsion, the dogs sit around Napoleon “wagging their tails at him in the same way as the other dogs had been used to do to Mr Jones” — a devastating detail showing that Napoleon has simply replaced one form of tyranny with another.

Squealer: The Voice of Propaganda

Squealer is Napoleon’s most important tool. Described as a pig who “could turn black into white,” Squealer represents the Soviet propaganda machine, particularly the state newspaper Pravda (which, ironically, means ‘truth’). After every new injustice, Squealer appears with “explanations” that twist reality. When the pigs take the milk and apples, Squealer claims it is for the animals’ benefit: “Do you know what would happen if we pigs failed in our duty? Jones would come back!”

Key Fact

Squealer uses several propaganda techniques: false statistics (“production has increased by 200 per cent”), appeals to fear (the threat of Jones’s return), rewriting history (claiming Snowball was always a traitor), and exploiting the animals’ inability to read or remember. Orwell shows that propaganda works not because it is believable, but because those in power control all sources of information.

After Snowball’s expulsion, Boxer adopts the personal motto “Napoleon is always right” alongside his existing “I will work harder.” This is one of the novella’s most poignant moments. Boxer is loyal, hardworking and trusting — exactly the qualities that make him vulnerable to exploitation. His blind faith in Napoleon represents how ordinary Soviet citizens accepted Stalin’s authority, partly out of genuine belief and partly because questioning the leader was dangerous. Orwell makes Boxer sympathetic precisely so the reader feels the injustice of his exploitation.

Rewriting History

One of Napoleon’s most insidious tactics is the systematic rewriting of the past. After Snowball’s expulsion, Squealer gradually transforms Snowball from a hero of the Rebellion into a traitor who was “Jones’s secret agent all the time.” The animals’ memories of Snowball’s bravery at the Battle of the Cowshed are replaced with a new version where Napoleon was the real hero and Snowball had actually been fighting on Jones’s side. This mirrors how Stalin had Trotsky’s image literally erased from photographs and official records. In the Soviet Union, history was not a fixed record but a tool of power — whoever controlled the narrative controlled the truth. Orwell shows that when citizens cannot verify facts for themselves, they become prisoners of whatever story those in power choose to tell.

The Windmill: Promise and Exploitation

In a typically cynical move, Napoleon reverses his position on the windmill after expelling Snowball. He announces that the windmill will be built after all — and claims it was his idea all along. Squealer explains that Napoleon only seemed to oppose it as a “manoeuvre” to get rid of Snowball. The windmill represents Soviet industrialisation under Stalin’s Five-Year Plans — ambitious projects that promised a better future but were built on the brutal exploitation of workers. The animals labour exhaustingly to build the windmill, but the pigs do none of the physical work.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Napoleon’s rise to power, focus on the methods he uses rather than just describing events. Napoleon succeeds through violence (the dogs), propaganda (Squealer), rewriting history (claiming the windmill was his idea), and eliminating opposition (expelling Snowball). For each method, make a clear link to how Stalin consolidated power in the Soviet Union. This demonstrates the contextual understanding (AO3) that Edexcel rewards heavily in Section B.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Snowball-Napoleon conflict mirrors Stalin vs Trotsky — Napoleon wins through violence and scheming, not through better ideas.
  • The dogs represent Stalin’s secret police; their use shows that Napoleon planned his violent takeover well in advance.
  • Squealer’s propaganda techniques — false statistics, appeals to fear, rewriting history — show how totalitarian regimes control truth itself.

lessons.title: Chapters 7-8: Terror & Purges
lessons.description: The confessions and executions, Boxer's unwavering loyalty, the changing commandments and the Battle of the Windmill.
lessons.content_html:
The Confessions and Executions

Chapters 7 and 8 represent the darkest phase of Animal Farm, mirroring the Great Purges of the 1930s under Stalin. Napoleon summons all the animals to the yard and, with the dogs snarling at his feet, demands confessions. One by one, animals step forward to confess to crimes they did not commit — or to minor acts of disobedience that are treated as capital offences. The hens who protested against giving up their eggs confess to “having secreted six ears of corn” and are slaughtered on the spot. The dogs tear the confessors’ throats out.

Key Fact

The confessions scene directly parallels the Moscow Show Trials (1936–1938), where Stalin forced former allies — including senior Bolsheviks who had fought in the Revolution — to publicly confess to treason, sabotage and conspiracy with foreign enemies. The confessions were fabricated under torture, but they provided a veneer of legality for Stalin’s mass executions.

Orwell describes the aftermath with devastating understatement: the animals huddle together on the knoll, and Clover looks down at the farm that was supposed to bring them freedom. “These scenes of terror and slaughter were not what they had looked forward to on that night when Old Major first stirred them to rebellion.” This is one of the most powerful moments in the novella — Orwell allows the reader to feel the gap between revolutionary hope and totalitarian reality.

Boxer’s Unwavering Loyalty

Boxer responds to every crisis with his twin mottos: “I will work harder” and “Napoleon is always right.” Even after witnessing the executions, Boxer does not question Napoleon’s authority. He believes the confessors must have been guilty, and he redoubles his physical labour. Orwell uses Boxer to represent the loyal, exploited proletariat who sustain the regime through their labour but receive nothing in return.

Boxer is arguably the most important character for understanding Orwell’s message. He is not stupid — he is trusting and decent, and those qualities are exploited by a regime that sees loyalty as a resource to be consumed. His physical strength literally builds the windmill (Soviet industrialisation), but Napoleon discards him the moment he is no longer useful. Orwell’s point is that totalitarianism destroys precisely the people whose hard work makes the state function. In the exam, you can argue that Boxer’s fate is Orwell’s most devastating critique of Stalinism.

The Hens’ Rebellion

Before the mass confessions, Napoleon orders the hens to surrender their eggs for trade with the outside world. When the hens refuse — in the only organised resistance in the entire novella — Napoleon cuts off their food rations. Nine hens die during the five-day standoff. This small but significant episode shows that Napoleon will starve his own citizens to enforce obedience, just as Stalin’s forced collectivisation of agriculture in the early 1930s caused the Holodomor — a devastating famine in Ukraine that killed millions. The hens’ protest is also notable because it is so quickly crushed. Orwell shows that individual resistance, however brave, is no match for a regime that controls food, information and armed force.

The Changing Commandments

Throughout these chapters, the Seven Commandments are quietly altered. “No animal shall sleep in a bed” becomes “No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.” “No animal shall drink alcohol” becomes “No animal shall drink alcohol to excess.” “No animal shall kill any other animal” becomes “No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.” Each addition of a qualifying clause strips away the original principle.

Key Fact

The changing commandments represent how authoritarian regimes rewrite laws and constitutions to legalise their own corruption. The Soviet constitution of 1936 — ironically written during the height of the purges — guaranteed freedoms that were systematically violated. Orwell shows that controlling language means controlling reality: if the commandments say the pigs can sleep in beds, then the pigs sleeping in beds is no longer a betrayal.

Frederick, the farmer from Pinchfield (representing Hitler and Nazi Germany), attacks Animal Farm and dynamites the windmill. The animals fight back and eventually repel the invaders, but at enormous cost — the windmill is destroyed. Napoleon declares it a “great victory,” which Squealer supports with propaganda. This parallels the German invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941 (Operation Barbarossa) and the devastating Battle of Stalingrad (1942–1943). The Soviet Union ‘won’ but suffered catastrophic losses. Orwell shows how totalitarian leaders reframe catastrophic defeats as triumphs.

‘Beasts of England’ Is Banned

After the executions, Napoleon bans ‘Beasts of England’ and replaces it with a new song praising Napoleon himself. Squealer explains that the song is “no longer needed” because the revolution is complete. This is deeply ironic: the revolution has clearly failed, and banning its anthem is Napoleon’s way of suppressing the animals’ ability to imagine a different future. The replacement song represents Stalin’s cult of personality — the state’s resources are redirected from collective ideals to glorifying the leader.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Chapters 7–8 contain some of the strongest material for an Edexcel essay. The confessions scene is powerful evidence for questions about power, fear, corruption or betrayal. When writing about it, avoid simply retelling the plot — instead, focus on what Orwell is showing about how totalitarian regimes maintain control: through terror, propaganda, and the systematic destruction of any opposition. Always connect back to the Moscow Show Trials and Stalin’s purges for AO3 marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The confessions and executions mirror Stalin’s Great Purges and Moscow Show Trials — fabricated confessions used to justify the elimination of opposition.
  • The changing commandments are a key structural device showing how revolutionary principles are rewritten to serve those in power.
  • Boxer’s blind loyalty represents the exploited working class — his trust enables the regime that will ultimately destroy him.

lessons.title: Chapters 9-10: The Betrayal Complete
lessons.description: Boxer's fate, the pigs in the farmhouse, the final commandment and Orwell's devastating conclusion.
lessons.content_html:
Boxer’s Fate: The Ultimate Betrayal

Boxer’s fate is the emotional heart of Animal Farm and Orwell’s most devastating indictment of totalitarianism. After years of backbreaking labour on the windmill, Boxer collapses. His lung gives out, and he can no longer work. The animals expect Napoleon to honour Boxer’s lifelong service by sending him to a veterinary hospital. Instead, a van arrives bearing the words “Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler.” Boxer is being sent to the knacker’s.

Key Fact

Benjamin, who has remained cynically silent throughout the novella, reads the lettering on the van aloud. The animals rush to the van, calling to Boxer. Boxer tries to kick his way out but is too weak. Squealer later claims the van had been bought by the vet but had not yet been repainted — a transparent lie. Napoleon uses the money from Boxer’s sale to buy whisky for the pigs.

Orwell makes Boxer’s fate so devastating because the reader has watched him give everything to the farm. His motto “I will work harder” represents genuine dedication, but it is exploited by a regime that values him only for his physical labour. The moment he can no longer produce, he is disposed of. This mirrors how Stalin’s regime worked Soviet citizens to exhaustion in the gulags and collective farms, then discarded those who could no longer contribute.

The Pigs in the Farmhouse

By the final chapters, the pigs have moved into Mr Jones’s farmhouse, sleep in beds, wear clothes, carry whips, and walk on their hind legs. Each of these actions directly contradicts the original Seven Commandments. The farmhouse, which was supposed to be “preserved as a museum” after the Rebellion, has become the pigs’ private quarters — just as the Kremlin, once a symbol of revolution, became the seat of a new autocratic elite.

The Seven Commandments are eventually reduced to a single statement: “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.” This is one of the most famous sentences in English literature. It is a paradox — a logical impossibility that exposes the absurdity and hypocrisy of the pigs’ regime. If some are ‘more equal’, then none are truly equal. Orwell distils the entire tragedy of the novella into this single sentence: the revolution that promised equality has produced its exact opposite.

The Final Scene: Pigs and Men

The novella ends with a scene of devastating dramatic irony. The pigs host a dinner party for the neighbouring farmers. Napoleon announces that Animal Farm will revert to its original name, Manor Farm. The watching animals look through the window: “The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.”

Key Fact

The final scene shows the pigs have become indistinguishable from the humans they overthrew. The cyclical structure is complete: Manor Farm became Animal Farm and is now Manor Farm again. The word ‘revolution’ literally means ‘a full turn of a wheel’ — Orwell suggests that without vigilance, revolution simply brings society back to where it started.

It is tempting to read Animal Farm as a purely pessimistic story — revolutions always fail, power always corrupts. But Orwell was a democratic socialist who believed change was possible. He was not arguing against revolution itself, but warning that revolutions must be protected by educated, vigilant citizens who hold their leaders accountable. The animals fail because they cannot read, they trust blindly, and they allow the pigs to monopolise information. Orwell’s message is directed at the reader: if you recognise these patterns, you can resist them. The novella is a warning, not a prophecy of inevitable doom.

Life Under the Final Regime

By the closing chapters, the animals work longer hours than they did under Jones, receive less food, and have no freedom whatsoever. The promises of retirement pastures and heated stalls have been quietly abandoned. Squealer reads out lists of figures proving that production has increased, but the animals’ lived experience tells them otherwise — they are hungrier and more exhausted than ever. This gap between official propaganda and everyday reality is a hallmark of totalitarian states. In the Soviet Union, state media celebrated record harvests and industrial output while ordinary citizens queued for bread. Orwell makes this contrast explicit to show that propaganda does not need to be believed to be effective — it just needs to be the only narrative available.

The Circular Structure

The novella begins and ends with tyranny. Mr Jones’s drunken neglect is replaced by Napoleon’s calculated cruelty. The animals have worked harder, sacrificed more, and ended up no better off than they were under Jones. The circular structure reinforces Orwell’s central argument: revolution without education, accountability and genuine equality will always be co-opted by those who seek power. For the Edexcel exam, discussing how Orwell uses structure to convey his message demonstrates the sophisticated understanding that distinguishes top-level responses.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The final chapters are essential for almost any Edexcel essay question on Animal Farm. Whether the question focuses on characters, themes, plot or settings, you can use the ending to show the culmination of Orwell’s argument. The key quotation — “it was impossible to say which was which” — works in essays about power, corruption, equality, revolution, or specific characters. Always analyse what it means in context: the pigs have become the humans they overthrew, completing the cycle of oppression. Connect this to the Soviet Union under Stalin resembling the Tsarist regime it replaced.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Boxer’s sale to the knacker’s is the novella’s most emotionally devastating moment — it shows how totalitarian regimes exploit loyal workers and discard them when they are no longer useful.
  • “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” — the final commandment distils the entire tragedy of the revolution into a single paradox.
  • The circular structure (Manor Farm → Animal Farm → Manor Farm) conveys Orwell’s warning that revolution without education and accountability will always be co-opted by new oppressors.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: In-depth analysis of Napoleon, Snowball, Squealer, Boxer, Old Major, Benjamin, Mollie, the sheep and Moses.
lessons.content_html:
Napoleon: The Cunning Dictator

Napoleon is Orwell’s representation of Joseph Stalin. He is described early on as “not much of a talker but with a reputation for getting his own way.” Unlike Snowball, who leads through ideas and persuasion, Napoleon leads through manipulation, violence and the slow accumulation of power. He takes the puppies and raises them as his personal enforcers. He lets Snowball do the intellectual work of planning the windmill, then steals the idea after expelling him. He has food tasters and surrounds himself with dogs at all times — details that mirror Stalin’s notorious paranoia.

Key Fact

Napoleon never contributes to the physical work of the farm. He does not build the windmill, fight in the battles, or produce anything useful. His only skill is the acquisition and maintenance of power. Orwell shows that dictators are fundamentally parasitic — they survive by exploiting the labour and loyalty of others.

Snowball: The Idealist Betrayed

Snowball represents Leon Trotsky. He is intelligent, articulate and genuinely committed to improving the animals’ lives. He organises reading classes, plans the windmill, and leads the defence at the Battle of the Cowshed. But Snowball is also naïve about power — he does not anticipate Napoleon’s willingness to use violence. After his expulsion, Napoleon rewrites history to make Snowball the villain, just as Stalin erased Trotsky from Soviet history and blamed him for every failure.

Squealer: The Propagandist

Squealer represents the Soviet propaganda machine, particularly the state newspaper Pravda. He is described as a “brilliant talker” who “could turn black into white.” His role is to explain, justify and rewrite reality to serve Napoleon’s interests. His techniques include false statistics, emotional manipulation, appeals to fear (“Jones would come back!”), and the systematic revision of history. Orwell suggests that propaganda is not just a tool of power — it is as essential to totalitarianism as violence itself.

Boxer represents the loyal, hardworking proletariat. His mottos — “I will work harder” and “Napoleon is always right” — make him both admirable and tragic. His physical strength builds the windmill and sustains the farm, but his blind trust in Napoleon leaves him vulnerable to exploitation. His sale to the knacker’s is the novella’s most emotionally devastating moment.

Benjamin, the donkey, represents the cynical intellectual who sees the truth but refuses to act. His catchphrase — “Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey” — suggests world-weary resignation. He can read as well as the pigs but never shares his knowledge. Only when Boxer is taken to the knacker’s does Benjamin finally speak out, and by then it is too late. Orwell uses Benjamin to criticise those who see injustice but remain silent.

Old Major, Mollie, the Sheep and Moses

Old Major represents Marx and Lenin — the visionary whose ideas inspire revolution but who dies before seeing what becomes of them. His speech is genuine and his vision of equality is sincere, but he provides no practical plan for preventing the corruption that follows.

Key Fact

Mollie, the vain mare who cares only about sugar and ribbons, represents the Russian bourgeoisie who fled to the West after the Revolution rather than accepting the new order. The sheep, who mindlessly chant “Four legs good, two legs bad” (later “Four legs good, two legs better!”), represent those who blindly repeat propaganda without understanding it. Moses the raven, who tells stories about “Sugarcandy Mountain” (a paradise after death), represents the Russian Orthodox Church — the pigs tolerate him because religion keeps the animals docile and hopeful.

Clover, the motherly mare, represents the ordinary working-class citizen who senses something is wrong but lacks the education or power to articulate it. After the executions, she looks down at the farm and reflects that “these scenes of terror and slaughter were not what they had looked forward to.” She cannot read well enough to check the commandments and must rely on what the pigs tell her. Orwell uses Clover to show how limited education keeps the working class powerless — a key contextual point about why Orwell valued democratic access to knowledge.

The Dogs: Instruments of Terror

The nine dogs are not characters in the traditional sense — they have no individual personalities, no dialogue, and no independent will. They exist purely as instruments of Napoleon’s power. Raised from puppies in isolation, trained to obey only Napoleon, they represent the NKVD (Soviet secret police) who enforced Stalin’s rule through intimidation, arrest and execution. Their presence at every public meeting ensures that no animal dares to question Napoleon. After the confessions scene, they sit around Napoleon “wagging their tails at him in the same way as the other dogs had been used to do to Mr Jones” — a detail that explicitly connects Napoleon’s regime to the tyranny it replaced.

Character Groupings for the Exam

When answering a character-focused question in the Edexcel exam, think about characters in contrasting pairs: Napoleon vs Snowball (dictator vs idealist), Boxer vs Benjamin (blind loyalty vs cynical silence), Squealer vs Old Major (propaganda vs genuine vision). Each pairing illuminates Orwell’s message from a different angle. Even if the question names one specific character, referencing others shows you understand the wider significance of Orwell’s choices.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Edexcel exam, character questions ask you to explore what a character represents as well as what they do. For every point about a character’s actions, add a sentence connecting it to the allegory and to Orwell’s purpose. For example, don’t just say “Boxer works hard” — say “Boxer’s relentless labour represents the exploitation of the Soviet working class, and his blind loyalty to Napoleon shows how totalitarian regimes exploit the very qualities that should make a society strong.” This kind of analysis scores highly on both AO1 and AO3.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Napoleon (Stalin) leads through violence and manipulation; Snowball (Trotsky) leads through ideas but is expelled and demonised.
  • Boxer (loyal proletariat) and Benjamin (cynical intellectual) represent two different responses to totalitarianism — both ultimately fail to prevent it.
  • Minor characters (Mollie, the sheep, Moses, Clover) each represent a social group’s response to revolution and dictatorship.

lessons.title: Allegory & Symbolism
lessons.description: Character-to-historical-figure mapping, the windmill, the commandments, the farmhouse and Sugarcandy Mountain.
lessons.content_html:
Allegory: The Layer Beneath the Story

Every element of Animal Farm operates on two levels: the surface narrative (animals on a farm) and the allegorical meaning (the Russian Revolution and Soviet Union). For the Edexcel exam, you need to move fluently between these two levels. When you discuss a character’s actions, connect them to their historical counterpart. When you discuss an event, explain what real-world event it represents and what Orwell is saying about it.

Key Fact

The key character mappings are: Old Major = Marx/Lenin, Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky, Squealer = Pravda (Soviet propaganda), Boxer = the loyal proletariat, Benjamin = cynical intellectuals, Mollie = the bourgeoisie, Moses = the Russian Orthodox Church, the dogs = secret police (NKVD), the sheep = citizens who repeat propaganda, Mr Jones = Tsar Nicholas II, Frederick = Hitler, Pilkington = the Western capitalist powers (Britain/USA).

The Windmill: Promise and Exploitation

The windmill is one of the novella’s central symbols. Snowball designs it as a project that will bring electricity, reduce working hours and improve the animals’ quality of life. After Snowball’s expulsion, Napoleon claims the idea as his own. The windmill represents Stalin’s Five-Year Plans — ambitious industrialisation programmes that promised to modernise the Soviet Union but were built on the brutal exploitation of workers.

The windmill is built, destroyed in a storm, rebuilt, destroyed by Frederick’s dynamite, and rebuilt again. Each cycle costs the animals more suffering while delivering less benefit. Orwell uses this repetition to show that the promise of a better future is the tool used to justify present suffering — and that the better future never actually arrives for ordinary citizens.

After the Rebellion, the animals agree that the farmhouse should be “preserved as a museum” — a symbol of the old regime that no animal should inhabit. But gradually, the pigs move in. They sleep in beds, eat from the best china, and eventually host dinner parties with humans. The farmhouse symbolises the Kremlin — once a symbol of revolutionary change, it becomes the private residence of a new elite. The distance between the farmhouse and the barn represents the growing gap between the rulers and the ruled.

The Seven Commandments: A Constitution Betrayed

The Seven Commandments function as Animal Farm’s constitution — the founding principles of the revolution. Their gradual alteration is Orwell’s most effective motif. Each change adds a qualifying clause that legalises the pigs’ behaviour: “with sheets”, “to excess”, “without cause.” The final reduction to “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” replaces seven principles with one self-contradicting statement. This mirrors the Soviet constitution of 1936, which guaranteed freedoms (speech, press, assembly) that were systematically violated during the purges happening at the same time.

Key Fact

Orwell shows that controlling language means controlling reality. If the commandments say the pigs can sleep in beds, then sleeping in beds is no longer a betrayal of the revolution. This connects to Orwell’s lifelong concern about political language, which he explored further in his essay ‘Politics and the English Language’ (1946) and in the concept of Newspeak in Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).

Sugarcandy Mountain: The Opium of the People

Moses the raven tells the animals about Sugarcandy Mountain — a paradise where animals go after death, where “it was Sunday seven days a week, clover was in season all the year round, and lump sugar and linseed cake grew on the hedges.” This represents religion, specifically the Russian Orthodox Church. Karl Marx famously called religion “the opium of the people” — a drug that numbs the working class to their suffering by promising rewards in the afterlife.

The pigs initially chase Moses away because he does no work and spreads distracting stories. But later, Napoleon allows Moses to return and even gives him a ration of beer. This parallels Stalin’s shifting relationship with the Russian Orthodox Church. Initially, the Bolsheviks persecuted the Church, but during World War II, Stalin rehabilitated it to boost morale and national unity. Orwell shows that totalitarian regimes will co-opt any institution — including religion — if it helps maintain control.

‘Beasts of England’: A Symbol of Lost Hope

The song ‘Beasts of England’ functions as a powerful symbol that tracks the trajectory of the revolution. Taught by Old Major, it represents the utopian dream of freedom and equality — an anthem that unites all the animals in shared hope. Its banning by Napoleon once he consolidates power is deeply significant: the dictator needs to erase the original vision of the revolution because it would expose how far the new reality has fallen from the original promise. The replacement song, which praises Napoleon personally, mirrors Stalin’s cult of personality, where art, music and literature were co-opted to glorify the leader rather than the collective ideals of socialism.

The Neighbouring Farms: The Cold War

Foxwood, owned by the easy-going Mr Pilkington, represents Britain and the Western democracies. Pinchfield, owned by the cunning, hard-driving Frederick, represents Nazi Germany. The shifting alliances between the farms mirror the complex diplomacy of the 1930s and 1940s — including the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 1939 (when Frederick and Napoleon briefly trade) and the subsequent German invasion (the Battle of the Windmill). The final scene, where Napoleon plays cards with Pilkington, represents the Tehran and Yalta conferences where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt divided up post-war Europe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about allegory and symbolism, avoid simply listing what each element represents. Instead, explain why Orwell chose these specific symbols and what they add to his argument. For example, the windmill is not just a symbol of industrialisation — its repeated destruction and rebuilding shows how authoritarian regimes use the promise of future prosperity to justify present suffering. This kind of analytical depth, linked to context, is what distinguishes Level 5 responses on the Edexcel mark scheme.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Every character, event and setting in Animal Farm has both a narrative function and an allegorical meaning — always work on both levels in your exam.
  • Key symbols: the windmill (industrialisation and false promises), the commandments (a betrayed constitution), the farmhouse (the privileges of the ruling elite), Sugarcandy Mountain (religion as a tool of control).
  • Orwell’s allegory is not a simple one-to-one mapping — it is a sophisticated argument about how power corrupts, propaganda deceives, and revolution can be betrayed.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Power, corruption, propaganda, class, revolution, education and loyalty explored with Edexcel exam technique.
lessons.content_html:
The Key Themes of Animal Farm

Almost every exam question on Animal Farm will connect to one or more of the novella’s central themes. Understanding these themes — and being able to discuss them with specific references to both the text and the context — is the foundation of a strong exam response. This lesson brings together the major themes and shows you how to structure an essay around them.

Theme 1: Power and Corruption

This is the central theme of the novella. Orwell shows that power, once acquired, will always corrupt those who hold it. Napoleon does not set out as a villain — he gradually becomes one as he accumulates more control. The famous quotation “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” distils this theme into a single paradox. Orwell’s argument is not that individuals are inherently corrupt, but that systems without accountability will always produce corruption. The pigs have no checks on their power: no free press, no independent judiciary, no educated citizenry to hold them accountable.

Key Fact

Key evidence for power and corruption: the milk and apples (early privilege), the dogs chasing Snowball (violence), the confessions and executions (terror), the pigs sleeping in beds (breaking their own rules), Boxer’s sale to the knacker’s (exploitation), the final scene with humans (becoming the oppressor). Each event shows power escalating and principles eroding.

Theme 2: Propaganda and Language

Propaganda is the mechanism by which power is maintained without constant violence. Squealer’s role shows that controlling language means controlling reality. When the commandments are rewritten, the rules change — and with them, the animals’ understanding of what is right and wrong. The sheep’s mindless chanting (“Four legs good, two legs bad”) shows how slogans replace thought. Orwell was deeply concerned about political language throughout his career — his essay ‘Politics and the English Language’ (1946) argues that dishonest language corrupts thought itself.

The revolution promises to abolish class distinctions — the seventh commandment states “All animals are equal.” But from the very first day, a new hierarchy emerges. The pigs assume leadership because they are “the cleverest.” They take the milk and apples. They move into the farmhouse. They wear clothes and walk upright. By the end, the class structure is identical to the one under Jones — a small elite exploiting the majority. Orwell shows that revolution without genuine structural change simply replaces one ruling class with another. This connects to the Soviet nomenklatura — the new ruling class who enjoyed luxuries unavailable to ordinary citizens.

Theme 4: Revolution and Its Betrayal

Orwell does not argue that revolution is inherently wrong. Old Major’s vision of equality is presented sympathetically, and the early days after the Rebellion are genuinely hopeful. What Orwell warns against is the betrayal of revolution — the process by which those who lead the revolution use their position to create a new tyranny. The cyclical structure (Manor Farm → Animal Farm → Manor Farm) shows that this particular revolution has come full circle, but it does not mean all revolutions must fail.

The animals’ inability to read is what makes the pigs’ deception possible. If the animals could read the commandments for themselves, they would see the changes. Clover senses something is wrong but cannot check the barn wall. Benjamin can read but refuses to share his knowledge. The pigs monopolise education: they teach their own piglets to read but do not extend this to the other animals. Orwell argues that an uneducated population is a vulnerable population — democracy requires citizens who can think critically and hold leaders accountable.

Key Fact

Theme 6: Loyalty and Exploitation. Boxer’s unshakeable loyalty (“I will work harder”, “Napoleon is always right”) makes him the novella’s most tragic figure. His loyalty is genuine and admirable, but it is exploited by a regime that values him only for his physical labour. When he collapses, Napoleon sells him to the knacker’s. Orwell shows that under totalitarianism, loyalty is not rewarded — it is consumed.

Exam Technique: Structuring Your Essay

For a modern-text essay, you will usually respond to a prompt — often a quotation or thematic statement — and write an extended argument. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, timing, and mark allocation. A strong response should follow this general structure:

Introduction: Address the prompt directly. State your argument clearly. Show you understand the theme or character the question focuses on. Reference Orwell’s purpose.

Main paragraphs: Each paragraph should make a clear point, support it with a specific reference from the text, and connect it to context where relevant. Use the pattern: Point → Evidence → Explanation → Context → Link back to the question. Make sure your paragraphs cover different parts of the novella — examiners want to see knowledge of the whole text, not just one section.

Conclusion: Return to the prompt. Summarise your argument. End with a statement about Orwell’s wider purpose or message.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Remember: Edexcel Section B tests AO1 (personal response + textual references), AO3 (context) and AO4 (SPaG). There are no AO2 marks in this section, so you do not need to analyse individual words or literary techniques in detail. Instead, focus on: (1) a clear, well-argued personal response that addresses the question throughout; (2) specific references to events, characters and quotations from across the whole text; (3) contextual connections to the Russian Revolution, Orwell’s political beliefs, and the historical period; (4) accurate spelling, punctuation and use of specialist vocabulary. Learn 8–10 key quotations by heart — in a closed-book exam, precise quotations make a powerful impression.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six key themes are: power and corruption, propaganda and language, class and inequality, revolution and its betrayal, education and critical thinking, loyalty and exploitation.
  • Every exam answer should weave together textual references, contextual knowledge, and a clear personal argument — use the Point → Evidence → Explanation → Context structure.
  • Learn 8–10 key quotations for the closed-book exam, and practise writing timed essays (50 minutes) to build exam stamina.
